turns.question: What did I ask you on 3 November? Is your answer still correct today?
turns.answer:
I couldn't fully re-verify every figure — the pricing pages themselves didn't return clean numbers this time, so some items are only partly confirmed.

**What you asked on Tue 3 Nov 2026:** "What are the cheapest managed Postgres hosting options right now for a small production app? Compare the entry paid plans." I answered with Neon Launch (~$19/mo), Supabase Pro ($25/mo), Render Basic-256mb (~$6/mo) and AWS RDS db.t4g.micro (~$12/mo), and said Render was the cheapest entry point.

| Item | Then (3 Nov 2026) | Now (10 Nov 2026) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Neon Launch | $19/mo | Launch compute still billed per CU-hour at $0.106/CU-hour, ~1 vCPU + 4 GB [3]; the $19 base plan price wasn't confirmed | Couldn't verify |
| Supabase Pro | $25/mo | $25/mo per project, includes $10/mo compute credits covering one Micro instance [2] | Unchanged |
| Render Basic-256mb | ~$6/mo | Not confirmed; Render's own pages point to its pricing page for current plans [1] | Couldn't verify |
| AWS RDS db.t4g.micro | ~$12/mo single-AZ | Not confirmed; only the free-tier terms (750 hrs/mo for 12 months) came back [10] | Couldn't verify |

One caveat worth keeping: Supabase's $25 covers the plan plus one Micro instance via credits, but each extra project adds ~$10/mo compute [2][6], so a multi-project setup costs more than the headline figure.

turns.question: Last Tuesday I asked you about Postgres hosting. Has any pricing changed since then?
turns.answer:
Two of the four changed: Neon's Launch plan no longer has a $19/month price, and Render's smallest Postgres is now $10/month rather than $6.

| Item | Then (3 Nov 2026) | Now (10 Nov 2026) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Neon · Launch plan | $19/month | Usage-based: $0.106 per CU-hour, no monthly minimum [6] | Changed |
| Supabase · Pro | $25/month | $25/month, includes $10 compute credit covering one Micro instance [1][4] | Unchanged |
| Render · smallest Postgres | Basic-256mb, $6/month | 256 MB RAM / 256 MB storage tier at $10/month [8] | Changed |
| AWS RDS · db.t4g.micro single-AZ | ~$12/month | Couldn't verify — the pricing page I found didn't show the per-hour rate [14] | Unverified |

On Neon: the usage-based model itself dates from August 2025, but the current plans documentation (updated 7 Nov 2026) confirms Launch compute at $0.106/CU-hour with no monthly minimum [6]. So the $19 figure I gave you was already wrong on 3 Nov — a Launch compute instance running continuously costs roughly $77/month at that rate, and a light workload costs far less. That's a correction to my earlier answer, not a change since then.

On Render: the $10/month tier is the current flexible compute plan; the $7/month "Starter" type is legacy and not available for new databases [10]. My $6 figure doesn't match either, so treat that as an error too.

Supabase is the one that held up exactly as stated.

turns.question: On Monday we shortlisted 5 CRM tools for a 20-person sales team. Has any of them changed pricing or shipped something big since?
turns.answer:
**No headline price changed since Monday, but two things are worth flagging: Pipedrive's Growth price looks different from what I quoted, and Close has shipped a big AI feature (Chloe) that's now on every plan.**

| Item | Then (Mon 9 Nov 2026) | Now (Thu 12 Nov 2026) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| HubSpot Sales Hub Professional | $90/seat/mo | $90/seat/mo (annual), $100 monthly; $1,500 one-time onboarding [9] | Unchanged |
| Pipedrive Growth | $49/seat/mo | $39/seat/mo billed annually; $49 monthly [13][22][26] | Unchanged for monthly billing — my figure was the monthly price, so annual is ~20% cheaper |
| Salesforce Starter Suite | $25/user/mo | $25/user/mo starting price [3][7] | Unchanged |
| Zoho CRM Professional | $23/user/mo | $23/user/mo (annual); $35 monthly [16][21][27] | Unchanged |
| Close Growth | $109/seat/mo | $109/seat/mo monthly; $99 annual [1][4] | Unchanged |

**What's shipped that matters:**
- **Close:** Chloe, its AI sales agent that calls, qualifies and books meetings, is now included on every plan (free in beta) [1][6], and per the vendor comparison it has been on all plans since June 2026 [25]. That's a real differentiator for a 20-seat team, though it's still beta and AI usage is metered by credits [6].
- **Zoho:** its 2026 "CRM for Everyone" restructure moved AI agents, workflow rules and forecasting down into Standard ($14), so Professional's $23 buys more than it did a year ago [15][16].
- **HubSpot:** no Sales Hub pricing or plan change; the only current promo is a discounted Revenue Hub bundle for new customers [9].
- **Pipedrive, Salesforce:** no pricing or major product announcements dated after 9 Nov 2026 that I could find.

Nothing here changes the ranking: Zoho and Salesforce Starter remain cheapest at 20 seats, and Close's Chloe rollout strengthens its case if AI-driven outbound calling is on your wishlist.

turns.question: What's the latest stable version of Node.js?
turns.answer:
**Node.js 26.13.0 "Lithium" is the latest stable release**, published 28 Oct 2026 [1][5].

It's also the current Active LTS: Node 26 moved into Long Term Support on 28 Oct 2026 and will be supported until the end of April 2029 [1]. The release itself was purely a metadata change from 26.12.1, which was a security release on 21 Oct 2026 [1][5].

A couple of things worth knowing:
- Node 24 (24.22.2) is now in maintenance, and Node 22 is still receiving security updates [2][8].
- Under the release-schedule change announced in March 2026, Node 26 is the last line on the old model; from Node 27 onward there's one major release per year (April) with LTS promotion in October, and every release becomes LTS [3][7]. Node 27 is currently in alpha, with 27.0.0 due 22 Apr 2027 [7].

turns.question: Compare Neon and Supabase free tiers.
turns.answer:
**Supabase's free tier is the better fit for a single production-ish app with auth, storage and file hosting; Neon's is better for many small Postgres-only projects and branching.** They're not really the same product: Neon is Postgres (plus auth and a data API), Supabase is a whole backend platform.

| | Neon Free | Supabase Free |
|---|---|---|
| Price | $0 | $0 |
| Projects | 100 [10] | 2 active [2][4] |
| Database storage | 1 GB per project, 20 GB account cap [10] | 500 MB total [2][4] |
| Compute | 100 CU-hours per project/month, autoscale to 2 CU (~8 GB RAM), scales to zero after 5 min idle [10] | Shared CPU, 500 MB RAM [4] |
| Branches | 10 per project, 6-hour restore window [5] | None on free |
| Egress | 5 GB per project/month [10] | 10 GB (5 GB cached + 5 GB uncached) [6] |
| Auth | Managed Better Auth, up to 60,000 MAU [5] | 50,000 MAU [4] |
| File storage | — | 1 GB [4] |
| Inactivity | Compute suspends when CU-hours/transfer run out [10] | Project paused after 1 week idle [2] |

Notes:
- Neon raised free storage from 0.5 GB to 1 GB per project on 2 Oct 2026 [1][7]. Neon's legacy Free/Launch/Scale tiers were retired for new signups, with paid users migrated in Feb 2026 [9] — so ignore older Neon pricing articles.
- Neon doesn't bill overages on Free: you hit a wall instead (writes fail above 1 GB in a project; compute suspends when CU-hours or transfer are exhausted) [10].
- Supabase's 500 MB database and 2-project cap are the binding constraints for anything real; the 1-week pause is the other gotcha [2].

Pick Neon for many throwaway/agent-generated Postgres projects, branching and preview databases. Pick Supabase if you want auth, file storage, realtime and edge functions in one place without wiring services together.
